title: India Flags Ultra-Processed Food Health Risks as ICMR Data Shows Rising NCD Burden
excerpt: A Union Health Minister's statement in Parliament cites ICMR research linking packaged food consumption to diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular disease as India's UPF market crosses $38 billion.
body:
• India's Union Health Ministry has cited ICMR research showing higher health risks from ultra-processed foods, including links to diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular disease.
  • India's UPF market grew at 13.37% annually from 2011 to 2021, reaching $38 billion — with each 10% increase in dietary UPF share linked to 14–30% higher cardiometabolic risk.
  • Over 40,000 food samples were found non-conforming in FY2025-26, with FSSAI stepping up enforcement through rapid testing kits and mobile laboratories.
  • Public health experts are pushing for mandatory front-of-pack warning labels, higher taxation on UPFs, and restrictions on marketing to children.

Government Acknowledges Growing Evidence

India's Union Health Ministry has flagged the rising health risks associated with ultra-processed food consumption, citing research by the Indian Council of Medical Research that draws a direct line between packaged foods and the country's escalating non-communicable disease burden. The statement, delivered during the current Parliament session, reflects growing government concern over a dietary shift that is reshaping India's public health landscape.

The ICMR-INDIAB study and related research have found statistically significant links between UPF consumption and diabetes, hypertension, and obesity. Regression models show that each 10% increase in the share of ultra-processed foods in the diet correlates with a 14–30% higher cardiometabolic risk. Diabetes prevalence in India has reached 11.4%, affecting an estimated 101 million people, while prediabetes stands at 15.3%, or 136 million.

A Market Growing Faster Than Regulation

India's ultra-processed food sector has expanded at a compound annual growth rate of 13.37% from 2011 to 2021, with market value rising from $0.9 billion in 2006 to $38 billion by 2019, according to Euromonitor data analysed in a comprehensive study published on medRxiv. Per capita processed food sales doubled from $31.30 in 2012 to $57.70 in 2018.

Sweet biscuits dominate with 43% of the market. Urban households increased their annual UPF purchases from 6.0 kg to 6.4 kg per person between 2013 and 2016. The Observer Research Foundation noted that UPFs are growing faster than staple or minimally processed foods, driven by convenience, long shelf life, and aggressive promotion by multinational corporations targeting emerging markets.

"If trends are not reversed, it would not take much time for India to reach a noncommunicable disease and obesity scenario now seen in developed countries like the United States and United Kingdom."

— Dr Arun Gupta, Nutrition Advocacy for Public Interest (NAPi)

Food Safety Enforcement Ramps Up

The government's concerns extend beyond nutrition to basic food safety. Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare Prataprao Jadhav informed the Lok Sabha that 223,808 food samples were analysed during FY2025-26, with 40,023 found to be non-conforming. The enforcement response included 31,878 civil penalties and 1,918 criminal convictions.

FSSAI has deployed mobile food testing laboratories, rapid analytical food testing kits, and a "Detect Adulteration with Rapid Test" handbook to help consumers and inspectors identify unsafe products. The recent Gujarat ban on analogue paneer and dairy substitutes signals a broader crackdown on food adulteration at the state level.

The NCD Crisis Deepens

Non-communicable diseases now account for 61.8% of all deaths in India, up from 37.9% in 1990. Cardiovascular diseases alone caused more than a quarter of total deaths in 2016, and premature NCD deaths doubled between 1990 and 2019. Between 2005–06 and 2019–20, adult overweight and obesity rates increased by more than 10 percentage points across both urban and rural populations.

An average Indian household now derives more calories from processed foods than fruits, according to a 2020 Lancet study. Clinical trials by the ICMR-Madras Diabetes Research Foundation have shown that diets high in ultra-processed and fried foods — rich in advanced glycation end-products — directly impair insulin sensitivity and elevate blood sugar levels.

Diaspora Health Implications

The research carries particular relevance for the Indian diaspora. South Asians are genetically predisposed to higher rates of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, and the shift toward processed diets accelerates that risk for families maintaining dual dietary habits across India and their countries of residence.

What's Next

A coalition of 29 Indian public health and consumer organisations has urged the government to mandate front-of-pack warning labels on high-fat, sugar, and salt products. The economic burden of diet-related NCDs is projected to reach $4.58 trillion by 2030. Whether India moves beyond awareness campaigns to implement taxation, stricter labelling, and marketing restrictions — particularly those targeting children through digital media — will determine whether the country can slow the trajectory that public health experts are calling a "health doomsday."
